passage:
"You've been quiet since the lab meeting. What happened?" Amandeep asked, dropping her bag on the hostel bed.
"Dr. Mehta gave the conference slot to Tanmay. His results are weaker. Everyone knows his cousin plays cricket with Dr. Mehta."
"Maybe there's a reason."
"Maybe. But my poster wasn't even mentioned. I used to copy how Dr. Mehta wrote problem statements. I thought everything about that was perfect."
"So are you going to tear up your notebook?"
"I almost did." Chandrika opened it and looked at the first page. "But the way of framing a question still works. That part is mine now, fair or not."
"And the slot?"
"I'll ask plainly why. And I won't decide that every professor is the same."

qa.q: What does Chandrika's remark about copying the problem statements suggest about how she felt before?
qa.a: She admired Dr. Mehta and thought everything about that work was perfect, so the letdown stings more.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do next about the conference slot?
qa.a: Ask Dr. Mehta plainly why Tanmay was chosen, while keeping the way of framing questions she learned.

qa.q: Why might Amandeep ask if she will tear up her notebook?
qa.a: Amandeep may worry that Chandrika will reject everything and everyone in authority, so the question checks that she is not throwing away useful learning.

grounding: A student finds her mentor biased, keeps what he taught and refuses to distrust all authority.

passage:
You know I worshipped Dr. Nirmala Pillai, Anju. In first year she's the reason I chose microbiology. She'd stay late explaining plating techniques; she lent me her own lab coat.
Then last month, in the lab meeting, she tore apart Revathi's presentation in front of everyone, and later I heard her say it was because Revathi had "sided with the other group" in some department quarrel. Petty. Really petty. And I realised she'd been giving the good projects to the people who flattered her.
For a week I was so angry I wanted to quit research. I told my roommate all professors are the same, just politics.
But then I was setting up a plate, and my hands did it exactly the way she taught me: careful, sterile, no shortcuts. That skill is real. It's mine now.
So I'm keeping the technique and dropping the pedestal. And I'm not giving up on every teacher because of one. I'm Keerthana, still a microbiologist, just less starry-eyed.

qa.q: What did Dr. Pillai lend Keerthana in first year?
How did Keerthana feel after the lab meeting?
qa.a: Angry and disillusioned, wanting to quit research and calling all professors "just politics".

qa.q: What did Keerthana decide to keep, and what to let go?
qa.a: To keep the careful technique Dr. Pillai taught, drop the pedestal, and not turn cynical about every teacher.

qa.q: How might Revathi have experienced the lab meeting?
qa.a: As humiliating and unfair, torn apart in front of everyone over a department quarrel.

grounding: Shows discovering that a mentor is petty and biased, keeping what she taught while updating one's view instead of rejecting all authority.

passage:
September: For two years, Ira had quoted her debate coach, Tejas sir, in every argument she had with anyone. He had taught her to build the other side's case first.
October: At selection for the national tournament, Tejas sir picked two debaters from his old school over Ira and Manav, who had beaten both of them in trials. In the corridor, Ira heard him say, "Those two just have the right polish." She went home and told her mother, "Adults are all fake. I'm done trusting teachers."
November: She still went to practice. One evening, preparing a case against a policy she liked, she caught herself doing exactly what he had taught: the other side first. The method was good even if the selection wasn't. She wrote to the department head, with the trial scores attached, asking how selections were made. She also thanked her history teacher, who had quietly told her to keep going.

qa.q: What had Tejas sir taught Ira?
qa.a: To build the other side's case first.

qa.q: How did Ira feel after hearing "Those two just have the right polish"?
qa.a: Hurt and disillusioned, declaring adults fake and giving up on trusting teachers.

qa.q: How did Ira avoid throwing away what she had learned?
qa.a: She kept using the other-side-first method, raised the selection formally with trial scores, and still trusted the history teacher who encouraged her.

qa.q: How might Manav feel about the selection?
qa.a: Unfairly passed over after beating both debaters in trials, and probably discouraged.

grounding: Illustrates disillusionment with a biased mentor over weeks, and keeping the learning while avoiding cynicism toward all authority.
